80:42.essay_html:
This is the last verse of the surah, and it names the people whose faces were just described as dust-covered and dark. "Those" points straight back to them.2,9,13 They are called al-kafara al-fajara, the plurals of kāfir (disbeliever) and fājir (one morally corrupt).2,3

The verse pairs two failings together. Kufr is corruption of belief, disbelief settled in the heart. Fujūr is corruption of speech and action, wrongdoing carried out. Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373 CE) reads the verse this way: disbelievers in their hearts, evildoers in their deeds.4,9 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE) adds a lexical note on fājir: some take it to mean the liar who fabricates against Allah, others the transgressor. Its root sense is inclination or deviation, so a fājir is one who has strayed from the path.3

Several commentators describe what this looked like in practice. These are people who disbelieved in Allah's favour, denied His signs, and dared to violate what He forbade.1,5,13 They treated the messengers and the Resurrection as false and disregarded the limits (ḥudūd) Allah had set, choosing instead to follow their own desires and turning away from the Prophet ﷺ.8,12,14 Ibn Kathīr notes a parallel elsewhere in the Qur'an, where a people is described as begetting "none but wicked disbelievers" (71:27), the same pairing of the two qualities.4

Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) reads the closing image of two kinds of faces, bright and dust-covered, as a mirror held up to two final destinies, so vividly drawn that the faces seem to move before the reader. He notes that this ending answers the surah's opening concern with values, now shown as the true scale by which people are judged.6 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976 CE) reads the close as a warning: those who persist in rejecting the message and opposing the Prophet ﷺ face a day of misery and shame, while the righteous have gardens of bliss and joyful faces.7 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021 CE) draws out that rejecting truth while remaining arrogant is the gravest of crimes, leaving such people with no worth in the Hereafter, while those who submit to the truth carry honour there.10

More than one commentator closes their reading of this verse with a plea of their own, asking Allah for pardon, and asking not to be counted among those it describes.5,9,12

80:24.essay_html:
The passage tells man to look at his own food, a simple thing, and trace it back to its source. Several commentators say this look is not just with the eyes but with the mind, tracing how food is made and delivered3, and some early exegetes read it even more literally, as looking at what enters the body and what leaves it1,2. A related report has the Prophet ﷺ pressing this same point on a companion: whatever he eats, however fine, ends the same way, a picture of how little this world is truly worth3. Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) draws out the deeper stake of the whole scene: watching dead earth come alive with growth is itself evidence that dead bodies can be brought back to life4, a reading echoed by several later commentators who tie the passage to gratitude and to preparing for what comes after1,3,5,9,11,12,13,14.

The chain begins with rain poured down from the sky in abundance, then earth splitting open so that seeds already inside it can sprout1,2,4,5,8,9,13. Readers of the Qur'an differ on a small grammatical point here, whether the following clause reads with a fatha or a kasra, which changes whether it directly continues the description of "his food" or opens a fresh sentence1,2,3,9. Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) brings in scientific ideas of his time about how water first covered the earth, cooling from vapour into rain and forming oceans, but he is careful to call these theories provisional, not something the verse depends on6.

From the wet, split earth grows every kind of grain1,2,3,4,5,9. "Qadb" is mostly explained as moist green fodder, cut again and again for grazing animals, also called qatt1,2,3,4,5,13,14, though some widen it to any vegetable that is cut and regrows, or fresh greens people themselves eat, such as cucumber3,9. Olive and date-palm are singled out for how many uses they give, one commentator noting dates alone are eaten and processed at several different stages of ripeness4,5,9.

"Ghulb," describing the gardens, comes from the same root as a thick neck, in a man or a lion, a word Arabic extends to trees thick in trunk or tightly grown together1,3,9. Exactly what it pictures is not settled: dense, intertwined trees, tall trees, fine noble palms, or trees thick at the middle, are all reported from the early exegetes1,2,3,4.

"Fakihah," fruit, is what people eat for pleasure; "abb" is the pasture animals graze that people themselves do not eat, a distinction reported widely1,2,3,4,5,9,11,12,13. Two well-known reports sit alongside this word. 'Umar b. al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه once recited this verse, asked himself what "abb" precisely was, then called his own question "takalluf," unnecessary over-reach, and told people to follow what is clear in the Book and leave what is not; Ibn Kathīr judges the chain for this report authentic1,2,3,4,9. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رضي الله عنه, asked the same question, refused to answer without certain knowledge, saying no sky would shade him and no earth carry him if he spoke of the Qur'an without knowing2,3,4,9. Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) reads their silence not as a ban on studying the Qur'an, but as putting gratitude for the favour ahead of pinning the exact plant, noting the word may simply have fallen out of everyday speech or covered more than one plant9.

The passage closes on "mata'an," enjoyment, a grammatical term marking all this produce as a benefit set out for both people and their livestock3,9. One commentator ties this directly back to resurrection: dead land brought to life by rain is the same parable used elsewhere for the dead being raised from their graves3. Another notes the enjoyment is only for an appointed term, after which a still greater event awaits6, and one observes that this closing line repeats, word for word, a verse from the paired sūrah al-Nāzi'āt8.

A chain that starts with rain falling from an empty sky and ends with grain, fruit and fodder on the table is offered here as proof enough of a power that can do what it likes with the dead earth, and, the commentators add, with the dead themselves.

80:1.title: He Frowned: The Blind Man and the Reminder
80:1.in_short: The Prophet ﷺ once frowned and turned away from a blind believer who came seeking to learn, because he was busy hoping to win over some leading men of Quraysh to Islam. God corrects him for this, teaches that a sincere seeker deserves attention before someone merely hoped-for, and then describes the Qur'an itself as a reminder recorded on honoured, exalted, pure pages carried by noble angelic scribes.

claims.text: The occasion of revelation: the Prophet ﷺ was speaking with a group of Quraysh leaders, hoping they would accept Islam, when the blind companion Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum came asking to be taught. claims.text: The blind man is identified as Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum (also given as Amr ibn Qays), a maternal relative of Khadījah رضي الله عنها, and an early, committed Muslim.

The identity of the Quraysh leaders present is not settled among the reports: they are variously named as Utbah and Shaybah (sons of Rabi'ah), Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas (not yet a Muslim at that time).

Al-Qurṭubī records that the Mālikī scholar Ibn al-ʿArabī rejected the identification of the rich man as Umayyah ibn Khalaf or al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah as baseless and ignorant, since both men stayed in Makkah, died disbelievers before or at Badr, and never went to Madinah, where Ibn Umm Maktum lived.

claims.text: Commentators draw a wider principle from the episode: no one should be singled out by rank in teaching or warning; the noble and the lowly, the rich and poor, master and slave, men and women, young and old are to be addressed alike, since guidance belongs to God alone.

Reports say that afterwards the Prophet ﷺ made a point of honouring Ibn Umm Maktum: greeting him with 'welcome to the one for whose sake my Lord reproached me,' asking whether he had a need, and appointing him twice as governor over Madinah in his absence; he was later seen at the battle of al-Qadisiyyah carrying a black banner.

Isrār Aḥmad draws a practical lesson: winning influential adherents can genuinely help a cause, but they must never be courted in a way that signals contempt for existing followers or cheapens the message; this balance is described as narrower than a hair and sharper than a sword's edge.

Kalla is a strong particle of rebuke and refutation; Sayyid Qutb notes this is the sole instance in the whole Qur'an of kalla used with this severity directed at the Prophet ﷺ, showing how weighty this standard is held to be.
'Innaha tadhkirah' - the pronoun 'it' refers to the Qur'an, or to this sūrah/this admonition: a reminder from God.

Sayyid Qutb reads the whole passage as establishing that a person's worth is measured only by God-consciousness (taqwā), not lineage, wealth, or power; even the Prophet ﷺ needed to be shown and corrected on this standard, which Wahiduddin Khan likewise reads here as: those the world counts prominent may have no value before God, while one who fears Him, though outwardly 'blind', is the one who is truly valued.
'Faman sha'a dhakarahu' means whoever wills, let him take heed of the reminder; some read the pronoun more widely, that whoever God wills, He grants understanding and heedfulness.

'Suhuf mukarramah' (honoured pages) is generally understood as al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the Preserved Tablet, honoured for what it contains; some, citing the mention of 'the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa' elsewhere in the Qur'an, took it instead as referring to the scriptures given to earlier prophets.

'Marfu'ah' means exalted in rank before God (one report, from Yahya ibn Sallam, took it to mean physically raised in the seventh heaven); 'mutahharah' means purified, kept from all defilement, so that only the purified may touch it.

claims.text: Mufti Muhammad Shafi explains 'mutahharah' to mean that people in a state of major or minor ritual impurity are not permitted to touch it.

The identity of the 'safarah' is disputed: most reports (from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd) say they are the angels, who act as intermediaries between God and His messengers; other reports say they are the scribes who record the revelation, or the reciters (qurra') of the Qur'an. Al-Ṭabarī judges the reading 'angels' most likely, since 'safir' means one who goes between parties to set things right, as the angels do between God and His messengers.

claims.text: A hadith states that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'The one who recites the Qur'an skilfully is with the noble, righteous scribes (the angels); and the one who recites it with difficulty, stammering over it, has a double reward.' Al-Qurtubi records this as agreed upon by Bukhari and Muslim, with the wording from Bukhari; Ibn Kathir records a version via Ahmad from Aisha رضي الله عنها.

80:1.essay_html:
The sūrah opens on a single scene. The Prophet ﷺ was speaking with some leading men of Quraysh, hoping his words might bring them to Islam, when a blind companion, Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, came asking to be taught. Reports differ on exactly who the leaders were, naming Utbah and Shaybah, Abu Jahl, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-Walid, or al-Abbas1,3,7,9 though al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) records that the scholar Ibn al-ʿArabī rejected naming Umayyah or al-Walid, since neither man ever went to Madinah where Ibn Umm Maktum lived3. The Prophet ﷺ frowned, in Arabic 'abasa, and turned away, tawalla, toward the visitors1,2,3,9. One report from Ibn Zayd adds that Ibn Umm Maktum himself pushed past his guide's attempt to hold him back, a discourtesy on his own side too1,3.

God speaks of this in the third person, 'he frowned', rather than addressing the Prophet ﷺ directly with 'you frowned'. Commentators read this as a mark of honour, softening a reproach that then turns, in the very next line, to direct and consoling address: 'what could make you know'7,9. The reason given is that this seeker might have been purified, yazzakka, or taken a reminder that would have benefited him1,2,5,9,13. Mufti Muhammad Shafi (d. 1976) reads these as two linked stages: purification for one already walking the path, and a growing awe of God for a beginner just starting on it7.

The self-sufficient man who was attended to, tasaddaa, is contrasted with him1,2,3,9. The Prophet ﷺ is told plainly that he carries no blame if such a man never purifies himself; his task is only to convey1,2,3,4,5,9,13. Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) draws from this a general rule: a certain, known benefit should not be set aside for an uncertain, hoped-for one5, and Mufti Shafi calls it a teaching principle in its own right, that reforming an existing seeker takes precedence over the uncertain hope of winning a doubter7.

By contrast, the one who came running, full of eagerness and fear of God, is the one from whom attention was withheld1,2,3,4,9, talahha, being distracted with something else1,3,9. Commentators draw from this a broad principle: no one, rich or poor, master or slave, should be singled out in teaching, since guidance belongs to God alone4,7,9,14. Reports say the Prophet ﷺ took this to heart afterward, greeting Ibn Umm Maktum with 'welcome to the one for whose sake my Lord reproached me', and appointing him twice as governor of Madinah1,2,3,7,9. Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) draws a fine practical caution from this: winning influential people to a cause is valuable, but never at the cost of making existing followers, or the message itself, seem cheap8.

The rebuke sharpens with kalla, a hard word of refutation. Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) notes this is the only place in the whole Qur'an where kalla carries such force directed at the Prophet ﷺ himself6. Qutb reads the entire episode as establishing a single heavenly standard of worth, taqwā, God-consciousness, over every earthly one of wealth or lineage, a reading Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021) echoes: the truly valued person before God may be the one the world overlooks6,10. 'This is a reminder', tadhkirah, whoever wills may take heed of it1,2,3,4,5,9,13.

The closing verses turn to describe this reminder's standing. It is set down in honoured pages, generally understood as the Preserved Tablet, though some point to the mention of 'the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa' elsewhere and take it to mean the scriptures of earlier prophets too1,2,3,4,5,7,8,13. These pages are exalted in rank, marfu'ah, and purified, mutahharah, kept from every defilement1,2,3,4,5,13; Mufti Shafi adds that this purity means people in ritual impurity may not touch it7. They are carried by safarah, go-betweens, understood by most reports as the angels who carry revelation between God and His messengers, though some read the word as scribes or reciters1,2,3,4,9,11. A hadith, recorded as agreed upon by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, ties this to the ordinary reader: the one who recites the Qur'an skilfully is with these noble, righteous scribes, and the one who struggles over it earns a double reward3,4,11. These carriers are kiram bararah, noble and truly obedient, from a root meaning one who is faithful to the truth1,2,3,9.

A blind man's simple request, and the Prophet's ﷺ momentary turning away from it, becomes in these verses the occasion for laying down how worth is measured before God, and for describing the Qur'an itself as a reminder carried on pages no less honoured, exalted, and pure.

80:38.essay_html:
The chapter closes on two faces, set side by side. Some will be bright that Day, others covered in dust and gloom. The split marks out the believers from the disbelieving, wicked evildoers.

Musfirah, the word used for the first group, means radiant, shining, like dawn breaking.1,2,3,9,4,13 Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923 CE) even draws out the root: 'asfara' describes a face turning bright, the same word used for daybreak, while a different, unrelated word describes a woman throwing off her veil.1 The commentators agree these are the faces of the believers, the people of Paradise, those with whom Allah is pleased.1,3,4,5,13 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE) collects several old explanations for the radiance itself: traces of hardship endured while striving in Allah's path, traces of ablution, or traces of night prayer, this last supported by a saying attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنه that whoever prays much by night finds his face made good by day.3 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976 CE) closes his own comment on the chapter by setting this radiant fate against the earlier warning of shame for those who reject the message.7 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010 CE) notes the same contrast of bright and gloomy faces had already appeared in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah.8 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021 CE) reads the whole scene as turning on one point: rejecting truth in arrogance is the worst of crimes, while submitting to it is what gives a person worth in the Hereafter.10

Laughing and rejoicing describe what that radiance carries. The laughter is joy at the bliss and honour Allah has given them; the rejoicing is hope for still more to come, the heart's gladness showing on the face.1,2,4,9,13 One note ties the joy to a specific cause: these are those given their record of deeds in the right hand, which leaves them certain of success.12 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) pictures these faces pouring light, confident their Lord is pleased with them, having been delivered from the terror of the deafening Blast named earlier in the surah, their outcome already made known to them despite all the surrounding horror.6

Ghabarah, dust, is what settles on the other faces, the faces of the disbelievers.1,3,9,4,13 Al-Baghawī (d. 1122 CE) and Sayyid Quṭb read this less as literal dirt and more as the blackness of grief, sorrow, regret and despair, the way anxiety visibly darkens a face in this world.2,6,12 Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) calls these people simply 'the wretched': black, dark, deeply gloomy, having lost hope of any good and recognised their own ruin.5 A report recorded by al-Ṭabarī, and relayed by al-Qurṭubī, says the very dust on these faces comes from the animals Allah turns to dust once judgement between them is finished.1,3

Qatarah, the darkness that then covers these faces, is close in meaning to ghabarah, an intensifying cover of gloom, eclipse and blackness.1,2,3,9,4 Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنه is reported to have read the phrase differently, as covered by disgrace and humiliation rather than only literal darkness.1,2,3,13 Ibn Zayd draws a fine distinction between the two dust-words: qatarah is the dust that rises and reaches the sky, carried on the wind, while ghabarah stays low on the ground, though he adds that in the end they come to the same thing.1,2,3 Al-Qurṭubī even brings a line of pre-Islamic poetry by al-Farazdaq, describing the dust-cloud raised by a marching army, to anchor the word's ordinary sense.3 These faces, the sources say, belong to those called 'the disbelieving, the wicked evildoers': disbelievers in heart, evildoers in deed, who denied Allah's blessings, rejected His signs, and dared to break His limits through wickedness and rebellion.4,13

Two faces, two fates: one bright with the joy of a promise kept, one dust-stained and darkened with the weight of what it denied.

80:33.essay_html:
The surah closes on the Hour itself. It opens with al-Ṣākhkha, the Deafening Blast, a word the commentators trace to a root meaning a hard, violent strike, so severe it all but deafens the ears.1,2,3,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 A few note a rival suggestion, that the word connects instead to listening intently, but al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) says the true sense in the language is the striking, deafening one.1,3 It is named as one of the Day of Judgement's own names, magnified by Allah as a warning, on the report of Ibn 'Abbās رضي الله عنه, and several read it as the second trumpet-blast after which the dead rise.1,3,4,7,8,11,13 Ibn al-'Arabī pointed to a paradox worth sitting with: a blast that deafens is also, in a sense, what makes one truly hear, because it deafens a person to this world while opening his hearing to the next.3 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) adds that the word's own harsh sound carries its meaning, and that this closing scene answers the surah's opening one, the fearful runner and the heedless man, beginning and end within a single design.6

On that Day a man flees, not towards his family but away from them: his brother, his mother and father, his wife, his children.1 Several reasons are offered, side by side, without any being preferred: he fears they will hold him to account for old wrongs between them; he does not want them to see the state he is in; or he simply knows they cannot help him, since "no protector will avail another" that Day.1,3,12 'Abdullāh b. Ṭāhir al-Abharī suggested something further: the fleeing itself is what makes their helplessness plain to him, and turns him instead towards the One who alone can lift such trouble, a truth he might have grasped in this world had it been shown to him then.3 One report, passed down through Ibn 'Abbās and Qatāda, names figures said to be meant here: Qābīl fleeing Hābīl, the Prophet ﷺ fleeing his own mother, Ibrāhīm عليه السلام his father, Nūḥ عليه السلام his son, Lūṭ عليه السلام his wife, Ādam عليه السلام the shame of his sons, though this is relayed rather than settled as the verse's one meaning.2,3

The order named, brother, then parents, then spouse and children, is read as rising through natural attachment, since a person is ordinarily more anxious for his spouse and children than for his parents, and for his parents than for a brother.4,7 Al-Zamakhsharī's reading, carried by al-Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010), hears the sequence as an escalation: he flees his brother, no, even his parents, no, even his wife and children, because none of them can avail him anything.9 Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) explains the flight simply by the weight of the moment: the horror is so great, the matter so heavy, that a person sees his own kin and turns away.4 He also carries a related hadith on intercession, where each great Messenger, asked to plead for creation, says only "myself, myself" — even 'Īsā b. Maryam عليه السلام will not ask even for Maryam who bore him; only the Prophet ﷺ answers "my community, my community".4,14 Sayyid Quṭb reads the fear throughout as inward: bonds that this world could never normally break are shattered by one cry, and a person, cut off from everything around him, is left with neither time nor strength for anyone but himself.6

This is what verse 37 names directly: each person that Day has a concern that fully occupies him, leaving no room for anyone else's affairs.1,2,3,4,5,8,9,11,12,13 A widely carried hadith has 'Ā'ishah or, in another telling, Sawdah رضي الله عنهما, asking the Prophet ﷺ how people would be resurrected. He told her: barefoot and naked. When she was alarmed at the thought of people seeing one another, he recited this very verse, meaning no one would be looking.1,2,3,4,9,11,12 Al-Qurṭubī also records a variant recitation, yaʿnīhi instead of the common yughnīhi, carrying the sense of a matter that turns a person away from his kin rather than merely occupying him.3 Al-Sa'dī (d. 1957) reads this total self-absorption as the hinge on which mankind splits into two, the fortunate and the wretched, a division the surah goes on to draw in bright and dust-covered faces.5,6 Wahīduddīn Khān frames the same moment as separating those who rejected the truth arrogantly, left with no worth that Day, from those who bowed to it, who alone carry honour there.10

A single cry undoes, in an instant, every bond a person once thought unbreakable, and leaves him with nothing but his own reckoning.1,4,6

80:17.title: Man's Creation, Death, and Ingratitude
80:17.in_short: God curses the ungrateful human being and traces his whole life story back to a single drop of fluid: shaped in the womb, given an easy path, made to die and be buried, and one day raised again. Despite this, man still fails to fulfil what he was commanded.

claims.text: "Qutila" (the opening word) means "cursed" or "driven from mercy" — man is described as cursed.

original_terms.gloss: cursed / driven away from mercy

claims.text: "Man" here means specifically the disbelieving man, following the rule that wherever the Qur'an says "qutila al-insān" or "fu'ila bi'l-insān" it refers to the kāfir.

A report identifies the occasion as ʿUtbah ibn Abī Lahab, who renounced belief after Sūrat al-Najm was revealed, was cursed by the Prophet ﷺ in prayer, and was later killed by a lion on a journey to Syria.

report.graded_by: not graded in the provided sources

claims.text: "Mā akfarahu" carries two possible senses: an exclamation of astonishment at the sheer intensity of his ingratitude despite God's abundant favours, or a rebuking question — "what made him disbelieve?"
Sayyid Quṭb reads "qutila" as a form of rebuke: man's deeds are so bad that a death sentence on him would not be surprising.
Ṭanṭāwī (citing al-Zamakhsharī) calls this verse a masterpiece of concision, combining the harshest blame with the briefest possible wording.
The question "from what did He create him?" is rhetorical, meant to expose man's humble origin against his arrogance and his refusal to acknowledge God's oneness and accountability.
Grammatically the sentence is a question in form, but its intended meaning is affirmation (taqrīr), not genuine enquiry.
Man is created from a nutfah, a lowly, insignificant drop of fluid — given as the reason he has no basis for arrogance.

original_terms.gloss: a drop of fluid, the seed of human life

claims.text: "Fa-qaddarahu" is read as: God shaped and proportioned his body through stages — nuṭfah, then ʿalaqah, then muḍghah — until his limbs and features (hands, feet, eyes) were fully formed.

An alternative sense of "qaddarahu": while man is in the womb, God decrees four things for him — his lifespan, his sustenance, his deeds, and whether he will be miserable or happy — based on a hadith transmitted through Ibn Masʿūd.

report.graded_by: Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ, citing agreement of Bukhārī and Muslim (al-Shaykhayn)

claims.text: Al-Ḥasan is reported to have remarked: how can man be arrogant, when he twice passes through the very path of urination?

Isrār Aḥmad gives a distinct reading: "qaddarahu" refers to man's shākilah — his innate disposition, formed from inherited traits and the imprint of his environment — comparing this to Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:84.

original_terms.gloss: one's innate disposition or personal mould

claims.text: One reading: "the path" made easy is the path of exit from the mother's womb at birth.

A second reading: "the path" is the path of good and evil, guidance and error — clarified for man and made easy for him to follow, comparable to "We guided him to the path, whether grateful or ungrateful" (76:3). Ibn Kathīr calls this the more correct reading.

A third reading (Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir, via al-Qurṭubī): God makes easy for each person the path toward what he was created and destined for, citing the saying "Act, for each is made easy toward what he was created for."
Al-Saʿdī combines both senses: God eased the religious and worldly means for man, guided him to the path, and tested him with command and prohibition.

Muftī Shafīʿ reflects on the wisdom of birth itself: the child develops through three layers of darkness hidden from the mother's own knowledge, and is then born through a narrow passage without undue harm to her.
"Aqbarahu" means God caused him to be given a grave, an honour, rather than leaving him exposed as carrion for birds and beasts, following al-Farrāʾ's explanation.

original_terms.gloss: caused him to be buried / given a grave

claims.text: A linguistic distinction is drawn between "qabara" (to bury with one's own hand — the qābir) and "aqbara" (to command or cause burial — God as the one who ordains it), illustrated with al-Aʿshā's verse and the anecdote of Banū Tamīm asking to bury Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.
The verse is taken to indicate the obligation to bury a dead human body; death itself is mentioned here as a divine favour, not a calamity, citing the saying "the gift of the believer is death."

report.graded_by: not graded in Muftī Shafīʿ's citation

claims.text: "Anshara" means to bring back to life; both "anshara" (transitive: God revives) and "nashara" (intransitive: he himself revives) are attested Arabic usages, supported by al-Aʿshā's poetry.

original_terms.gloss: He brought him back to life

claims.text: "Whenever He wills" signals that the resurrection occurs by God's will alone and at the time He chooses, regardless of anyone who demands it sooner.

Ibn Kathīr links this verse to parallel Qur'anic passages (30:20, 2:259) and to a hadith stating that the whole of the human body decays except the tailbone, from which man will be reconstructed — reported from Abū Hurayrah in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.

report.graded_by: Ibn Kathīr, citing agreement of Bukhārī and Muslim

claims.text: The same hadith about the surviving tailbone, together with a report on the interval between the two trumpet-blasts, is cited from Abū Hurayrah via Bukhārī and Muslim.

report.graded_by: Bukhārī and Muslim, as cited by Abū Bakr Zakariyyā

claims.text: The underlying argument: the same power that brought man into existence out of nothing can just as easily bring him back after death.
"Kallā" rebuts man's claim to have fulfilled God's rights upon him — in truth he has not discharged what he was commanded.

original_terms.gloss: no! / not at all — a word of rebuttal

claims.text: Mujāhid and Qatādah: no one ever fully discharges everything that was made obligatory upon him.
Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have explained "he has not fulfilled what he was commanded" as referring to the covenant taken from him in the loins of Adam.
Al-Ḥasan reads "kallā" as meaning "truly" (ḥaqqan) rather than as a rebuttal.

Ibn Kathīr's own preferred reading, differing from al-Ṭabarī, is that the phrase refers forward to the resurrection just mentioned: it has not yet taken place, and will not, until the decreed span of humanity's earthly existence is complete.
Al-Saʿdī: despite everything God has done for him, man does not carry out what he was commanded, and remains perpetually short of what is demanded of him.
A grammatical note on recitation pauses (waqf): stopping at "kallā" is considered poor style; it is better to pause after "amarahu" and "nasharahu", in which case "kallā" carries the sense "truly".

Wahiduddin Khan: true godliness is driven by gratitude; serious reflection on one's own creation and the natural order surrounding it should produce a sense of gratitude toward one's Lord, and that gratitude is what real devotion consists of.

80:17.essay_html:
The passage opens with a curse: 1,2,3,4,9,13,14 "qutila" (قُتِلَ) means cursed, driven from mercy. The commentators take "man" here to mean specifically the disbelieving man, following a rule Mujāhid stated for the whole Qur'an: wherever it says "qutila al-insān" it means the kāfir.1,3,4 One report ties the verse to ʿUtbah ibn Abī Lahab, who renounced belief after Sūrat al-Najm was revealed and was later killed by a lion, though this remains an unrated historical report.2,3 "Mā akfarahu" is read either as astonishment at the sheer scale of his ingratitude, or as a rebuking question — what made him disbelieve?1,2,3,9 Sayyid Quṭb takes the opening word itself as rebuke: man's conduct is bad enough that a death sentence on him would be no surprise.6 Ṭanṭāwī, citing al-Zamakhsharī, calls the line a model of concision, the harshest blame carried in the fewest words.9

The next question — "from what did He create him?" — is not asked for information. It is meant to expose man's humble origin against his arrogance, his refusal to acknowledge God's oneness and his accountability.1,2,3,7,9 Grammatically it is a question; its real force is confirmation.2 The answer follows at once: a nuṭfah, a drop of fluid, hardly the material from which pride should grow.1,3,5,6,7,9,11,12,14 "Faqaddarahu" is read as God shaping that fluid through stages — nuṭfah, then ʿalaqah, then muḍghah — until every limb and feature is set in place.1,2,3,4,7,11,12 A second sense of the same word is decree: while still in the womb, God settles four things for the person — lifespan, sustenance, deeds, and whether he will be happy or wretched, a reading resting on a hadith transmitted through Ibn Masʿūd and graded sound by agreement of Bukhārī and Muslim.4,7,11 Al-Ḥasan is reported to have asked how man can be arrogant when he twice passes through the very path of urination.3 Isrār Aḥmad reads "qaddarahu" differently again, as the shaping of man's shākilah — his inborn disposition, formed from inherited traits and the mark of his surroundings, comparing this to 17:84.8

"Then He made the path easy for him" draws two main readings. Many commentators take "the path" as the path out of the mother's womb, made easy at birth.1,2,3,4,7,8,9,11,12,14 Others, including Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd, take it as the path of good and evil, of guidance and error, clarified for man and made easy to follow — comparable to "We guided him to the path, whether grateful or ungrateful" (76:3). Ibn Kathīr calls this the more correct reading.1,2,3,4,5,6,9,11,12,14 A further reading, attributed to Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir, takes it as God easing for each person the path toward what he was created for.3 Al-Saʿdī combines the strands: God eased both the religious and worldly means, guided man, and then tested him with command and prohibition.5 Muftī Shafīʿ lingers on the wonder of birth itself — a child forming through three layers of darkness unknown even to its own mother, then emerging through a narrow passage without harming her.7

Death follows, and then burial. "Aqbarahu" is explained, following al-Farrāʾ, as God granting man a grave — an honour, sparing him from being left exposed to birds and beasts.1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9,11,12,14 The commentators draw out a fine linguistic point: "qabara" is to bury with one's own hand, while "aqbara" is to command or cause burial — so it is God who ordains that man be buried, illustrated with al-Aʿshā's poetry and an anecdote of Banū Tamīm asking permission to bury the slain Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.1,2,3 Muftī Shafīʿ takes this as pointing to the obligation to bury the dead, and reads death itself here as a favour rather than a calamity, citing the saying that death is the gift of the believer.7

"Then, when He wills, He raises him again." "Anshara" means to restore to life; both the transitive and intransitive forms of the word are attested in Arabic usage.1,3 The phrase "whenever He wills" places the timing of resurrection entirely in God's hand, not to be hurried by anyone demanding it.9 Ibn Kathīr connects the verse to other Qur'anic passages on resurrection and to a hadith, reported from Abū Hurayrah in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, that the whole human body decays except the tailbone, from which it will be reconstructed — a hadith also cited elsewhere with a note on the interval between the two trumpet-blasts.4,11 The underlying reasoning, given by several commentators, is simple: the same power that brought man out of nothing can bring him back after death.5,6,8

The section closes on a rebuttal. "Kallā" — no — answers man's claim to have fulfilled what God asked of him: in truth he has not.1,2,3,4,9,13,14 Mujāhid and Qatādah held that no one ever fully discharges everything made obligatory on him.1,3 Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have tied the unfulfilled command to the covenant taken from every soul in the loins of Adam.3 Al-Ḥasan read "kallā" not as rebuttal but as "truly", a reading with its own grammatical support in where the recitation should pause.2,3 Ibn Kathīr, departing from al-Ṭabarī, took the phrase to point forward: the resurrection just mentioned has not yet happened, and will not, until the appointed span of human life on earth runs its course.4 Al-Saʿdī summed up the human condition plainly: for all that God has done, man still falls short of what is asked of him.5 Wahiduddin Khan draws the wider lesson: real godliness grows out of gratitude, and gratitude is what serious reflection on one's own creation is meant to produce.10

A single drop of fluid, shaped, guided, buried with honour, and one day raised again — set against a creature who, for all that, has not yet done what he was told.
